sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Rhode Island, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Tuesday, October 13Passed

The deadline for a regular mail ballot was 4 p.m. on Tuesday, October 13, 2026 (the law says 21 days before the election; an application postmarked by then and received by October 16 also counted). That deadline has passed. An emergency mail ballot application can still be made until 4 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026 (the day before the election). (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must be received by the State Board of Elections by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026 (when the polls close). A postmark is not enough. (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Rhode Island’s own site

At school away from home, in Rhode Island or in another state? What Rhode Island says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. State law lets any registered voter choose to vote by mail "for any reason". (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Apply on the Secretary of State's mail ballot portal. You need your date of birth and your Rhode Island driver's license or state ID number. The deadline for a regular mail ballot has passed (see below). Open it (the law)
  • By mail. Fill in the paper mail ballot application and get it to your city or town's local board of canvassers by mail or in person. The deadline for a regular mail ballot has passed (see below). Open it (official page)
  • In person. From now until the day before the election, you can still ask for an emergency mail ballot. Get the application from your city or town's local board of canvassers (you can also fill it in on an electronic poll pad there). It must reach the board by 4 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026. You can vote the ballot right there, or have it mailed to an address in the United States, or have someone you authorize in writing pick it up. (the law)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it in the envelope addressed to the State Board of Elections in Cranston. It must arrive by 8 p.m. on Election Day. (the law)
  • Drop box. Every city and town has at least one official mail ballot drop box, and there are boxes outside the Board of Elections and the Secretary of State's office. Boxes open 35 days before the election and take ballots until the polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day. A ballot put in a drop box by then counts as received on time. Open it (the law)
  • In person. An emergency mail ballot can be returned to your local board of canvassers or an official drop box by 8 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)

What the envelope needs

No witness or notary is needed. You sign the statement on the certifying envelope yourself, swearing you are a citizen and a Rhode Island voter and that you marked the ballot. If you cannot sign because of blindness, a disability, or not being able to read or write, the person who helps you marks a box and writes their name, address and signature. (the law)

Vote early in person instead

Wednesday, October 14, 2026 to Monday, November 2, 2026.

Any voter who cannot vote at their polling place on Election Day can vote early in person during the 20 days before the election, Wednesday, October 14 through Monday, November 2, 2026, usually at the city or town hall or another place the local board chooses. You show a photo ID, as at the polls. Days and hours differ from town to town; the Board of Elections posts the list. Early voting must be done in the city or town where you live. (official page)

Where to vote early

Students

At school in Rhode Island, away from home

The Board of Elections' pages do not speak to students separately. State law says your voting residence is your settled home, the place you are regularly present and mean to live for an indefinite time, and you can have only one. It also says you do not lose that home just because you are away as a student at a school. A student who keeps their home town as their voting address can get a mail ballot sent to any address in the United States, such as a school address. (the law)

At school in another state, with Rhode Island as home

State law says you do not lose your Rhode Island voting home just because you are away attending a school, and a mail ballot (for any reason) can be sent to any address in the United States. The state's pages do not say more about students. The regular mail ballot deadline (October 13, 2026) has passed. (the law)

Military and overseas

Members of the military, their spouses and dependents, and citizens living outside the United States can use the federal card (the FPCA) to ask for a ballot, with no witness or notary needed. State law says the card must reach the local board of canvassers (or the Secretary of State, if sent electronically) by the regular mail ballot deadline, 4 p.m. on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, which has passed. Their ballots count if received by the State Board by 4 p.m. on the seventh day after the election (Tuesday, November 10, 2026). Ballots can be sent and returned electronically through the Secretary of State. The Federal Voting Assistance Program explains the federal forms. (the law)

Rhode Island in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • If you applied for a mail ballot, you cannot trade it in for an early in-person ballot. You either return the mail ballot or vote a provisional ballot at your polling place on Election Day.
  • The seventh-day deadline for military and overseas ballots is in state law 17-20-16 (source 4); the federal card and no-witness rule are in 17-20-6.1 (source 10).
  • The FPCA deadline (the regular mail ballot deadline) is in state law 17-20-6.1 (source 10) read with 17-20-2.1 (source 1).

How this was checked

  • The Secretary of State's voter site (vote.sos.ri.gov) answered our request with a check for human visitors, so it was not read. We could not confirm the address of an official ballot tracker, so none is given; your local board of canvassers or the Board of Elections (401-222-2345) can tell you your ballot's status.
  • The FVAP page loads by script and could not be read; it is linked, not quoted. Military and overseas facts here come from state law.
